0.title: Waiting for His Son from Heaven
0.overview:
First Thessalonians is probably the earliest of Paul’s letters preserved in the New Testament — penned from Corinth around AD 50–51, within just weeks or months of his departure from the Thessalonian church. It is a letter warm with affection, urgent with concern, and radiant with hope. More than almost any other letter in the Pauline corpus, it vibrates with the pulse of a young church under pressure and a pastor who loves them like a father, a mother, and a brother all at once.

The city of Thessalonica was the capital of the Roman province of Macedonia — a major port, a commercial hub, a city full of every religion Rome and the East could offer. Paul had arrived there on his second missionary journey, preached for perhaps three weeks in the synagogue, and watched as a community of faith was born — Jewish converts, god-fearing Greeks, and not a few prominent women (Acts 17:1–9). Then a riot broke out, the city authorities were alarmed, and Paul was smuggled out by night. He never forgot those he had left behind.

The letter's great themes weave together like threads in a tapestry. There is the gospel — how it arrived in Thessalonica not merely as words but in power, in the Holy Spirit, in full conviction (1:5). There is the church as a community shaped by faith, hope, and love — Paul's great triad appears here earlier than in 1 Corinthians 13. There is holiness — the call to sanctification, especially in the realm of sexual purity, that flies directly in the face of Greco-Roman culture. And there is the return of Christ — the parousia — which dominates the last two chapters and gives the whole letter its eschatological urgency. The Thessalonians were grieving for those who had died before Jesus returned; Paul's answer is the most vivid description of the Second Coming in all of Scripture.

Above all, this is a letter about hope. Not the vague optimism the world calls hope, but the taut, muscular, resurrection-grounded hope that transforms how believers grieve, how they work, how they treat their bodies, and how they face the future. 'We do not want you to be uninformed, brothers, about those who are asleep,' Paul writes, 'so that you may not grieve as others do who have no hope' (4:13). That contrast — hope versus hopelessness — is the heartbeat of 1 Thessalonians. The God who raised Jesus will raise them. The Lord who ascended will descend. The church that suffers now will be presented blameless before him at his coming.

1.title: The Gospel That Works
1.overview:
This is probably the earliest letter in the New Testament, written around AD 50 from Corinth. Paul had preached in Thessalonica, capital of Macedonia, for only a few weeks before a riot forced him out by night (Acts 17:1–10). He had been frantic about the young church he left behind, and chapter 1 is his relief and thanksgiving at the news that they are standing.

He thanks God for their faith that works, love that labours and hope that endures. He knows God chose them, because the gospel came to them with the Spirit’s power and changed them. They received it with joy in the middle of persecution, and the story of their conversion has spread across Greece: they turned from idols to serve the living and true God, and to wait for his Son from heaven, Jesus, who rescues us from the coming wrath. Turned, serving, waiting: the whole Christian life in ten verses.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The letter opens with the names of the three missionaries who founded the church, Paul, Silas and Timothy, and greets the Thessalonian believers as a congregation whose life is rooted in God the Father and the Lord Jesus, wishing them grace and peace.
verseByVerse.theology:
Joining the Father and the Lord Jesus as a single source of grace and peace is a compressed Christology, and its date is what makes it startling. This letter is very likely the earliest document in the New Testament, written around twenty years after the crucifixion — well before any Gospel. There was no long development during which a human teacher was gradually elevated to divine status. The highest view of Christ is already here, in the first line of the first thing written, stated as though it needed no defence.

The Reformed tradition, with Nicaea, has always insisted that a creature cannot be a co-source of divine blessing. Grace and peace come from God; if they come from Jesus in the same breath and under the same preposition, then Jesus is not on the creature side of the line. The greeting is a doxology in miniature: two persons, one blessing.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: In Thessalonica, kyrios was Caesar's title, and the city was proud of its standing with Rome — a free city that had backed the winning side and kept its own assembly for it. Acts records the charge laid against these believers exactly: they say there is another king, Jesus (Acts 17:7). To receive a letter greeting them from the Lord Jesus was to be reminded whose throne their welfare actually came from.

Now: Notice what Paul does not put in his greeting. No title, no credentials, no reminder of what he had done for them. Where he was loved and trusted he simply used his name. It is a small thing, and it is a fair question for anyone who holds office in a church: how much of your authority do you find you have to keep asserting, and why?

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy, To the church of the Thessalonians in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ: Grace to you and peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy, To the church of the Thessalonians in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ: Grace to you and peace.

Meaning first. 1 Thessalonians is one of Paul’s earliest letters, very possibly the first thing in the New Testament to be written down, sent to a young church that had been planted in a few weeks and then left suddenly under persecution. Paul writes to encourage them, to answer slanders against him, to teach them holiness, and to comfort them about believers who had died before Christ’s return. Chapter 1 is a thanksgiving. Paul remembers their work of faith, labour of love and steadfastness of hope (vv. 1–3). He knows God chose them, because the gospel came to them not only in words but with power, the Holy Spirit and deep conviction (vv. 4–5). They received the word with joy in spite of suffering, imitated Paul and the Lord, and became an example to believers everywhere; their faith became famous (vv. 6–8). Everyone talks of how they turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God, and to wait for his Son from heaven, Jesus, who rescues from the coming wrath (vv. 9–10). The chapter is a portrait of genuine conversion, and every line of it is a portrait of what God does, not of what clever people manage.

The setting. Thessalonica was the capital of Macedonia and a busy port on the great Roman road, the Via Egnatia, which ran across the province from the Adriatic to Byzantium. Paul, Silas and Timothy came there from Philippi, where Paul and Silas had been beaten with rods and jailed (Acts 16–17). They reasoned in the synagogue on three Sabbath days (Acts 17:2), and some Jews and a great many God-fearing Greeks believed. Then jealous men gathered a mob, dragged Paul’s host Jason before the city authorities, and the believers sent Paul and Silas away by night (Acts 17:5–10). Perhaps a month, perhaps a little more, and he was gone, leaving these people on their own in a hostile city with almost no teaching and no apostle. Paul, frantic for them, sent Timothy back; Timothy’s good report prompted this letter, written from Corinth around AD 50–51 (3:1–6; Acts 18:5). What it contains is not a treatise but the relief of a man who had been sick with worry about a congregation he had been forced to abandon.

Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy. Notice what is missing. Paul does not call himself an apostle. In Galatians the first line insists on it, because his authority was under attack there; to the Corinthians the same. Here, nothing: just his name, alongside two others. Where he is loved and trusted he does not need the title, and he does not use it, which is a small thing worth noticing in a man often accused of being high-handed. Silvanus is the Silas of Acts (Acts 15:40), the man whose feet were fastened in the stocks beside Paul’s in the Philippian jail and who sang hymns with him at midnight (Acts 16:24–25). Timothy is the young man from Lystra who will be sent back to Thessalonica alone, at some risk, in chapter 3. All three had been in the city together. Paul writes as one of a team, and he means it.

To the church of the Thessalonians in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. The word church (ekklēsia) was the ordinary Greek word for a city’s civic assembly, the gathering of citizens called out to do the town’s business. Thessalonica had one of those already. Paul gives the same word to a scattering of former idol-worshippers and synagogue attenders, weeks old, meeting in somebody’s house in a town that had just run their teacher out, and then he tells them where they actually live. Not the church at Thessalonica, as though the city were what defined them, but the church of the Thessalonians in God. One small preposition carries the whole weight: they are located in God. Their address on earth was hostile; their address in heaven was the Father’s own life.

The Father and the Son under one preposition. The two names are joined, the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ together, as the single sphere in which the church lives, and Paul offers not a word of explanation. No Jew raised on the Shema, the confession that the LORD our God is one, does that casually. This is one of the earliest Christian sentences we possess, written about twenty years after the cross, and it already places Jesus on the divine side of the line, not by argument but by instinct. The church did not slowly promote a Galilean teacher to deity over centuries. From the first letter, the risen Jesus is named with the Father as the one in whom his people live.

Grace to you and peace. This is the shortest of Paul’s greetings, and the order never varies, because it cannot. Grace is the unearned favour that comes down from God; peace is what it makes when it lands, peace with God and then the settled wholeness of a life put right. A church under pressure needs both, and in that order. Peace without grace is a truce that will not hold; grace always arrives carrying peace in its hands.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the church was a mere civic club, one more association among the trade guilds and burial societies of a Greek city. It was gathered by God, in God, and that is why the city could not dissolve it by running its preacher out of town.

What does it mean for a church to be in God? It means its existence and security rest in him, not in its numbers, building, reputation or leaders. A church in God is held by the Father’s care and joined to Christ as a body to its head, so its life comes from him and cannot be ended by the people who oppose it. Practically, it frees a small or struggling congregation from measuring itself by what the town thinks. The Thessalonian believers had no building, no history and no apostle, and Paul still addresses them as an assembly whose true location is the Father and the Son. Your church, however ordinary its Sunday looks, is that too.

Why does Paul leave out his apostleship here? Because nothing in Thessalonica required him to defend it. His authority was not in question, so he simply wrote as a friend alongside his fellow workers. It is a quiet lesson for anyone with a title: use it when the truth needs defending, and set it aside when love can do the work without it. Authority in the church is a trust for the good of others, not a badge to wear.

In a sentence. From Paul, Silas and Timothy, to the church of the Thessalonians in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ: grace and peace to you.

On a Tuesday. Your church lives in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, whatever its address, its size or its troubles. When you are tempted to despise it, or to despair of it, name to yourself where it really lives. Then thank God for it, by name, and pray for it today.

For worship. Blessed be the Father who gathers a church out of a riot, and the Son who is named with him in the same breath. Blessed be the God who gives a weeks-old congregation, with no building and no teacher, an address no mob can reach. Grace comes down from him, and peace follows it, and both were bought by the Son in whom his people live.
verseByVerse.note: Thessalonica was the capital of Macedonia and a busy port on the Via Egnatia, Rome’s great east–west road. Paul founded the church on his second journey but was soon driven out. Silvanus is the Silas of Acts. Paul probably wrote from Corinth around AD 50, making this one of his earliest letters.

verseByVerse.ref: 1:2–10 – Faith, Love, Hope — and a Church Everyone Was Talking About
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul tells them he never stops thanking God for them, remembering faith that shows itself in action, love that puts in hard work, and hope in Christ that keeps going. He is confident God has chosen them, because the gospel reached them with the Spirit’s power and deep conviction, and they saw how the missionaries lived. They welcomed the message in the middle of persecution, with a joy only the Spirit gives, and so became a pattern for believers across Macedonia and Achaia. People everywhere talk about how they abandoned idols to serve the true God and now wait for his Son, whom God raised, to come from heaven and rescue them from the judgement to come.
verseByVerse.theology:
Election, and How Anyone Could Know

Verse 4 states election flatly and warmly, and verse 5 gives the grounds. Paul claims no private glimpse of the eternal register. He reasons from effect to cause: the gospel arrived among these people with power, the Spirit, and settled conviction, and it produced work, labour and endurance — therefore God had chosen them. The hidden decree becomes visible in time through the effectual call. Peter puts the order exactly: we make our calling and election sure (2 Pet. 1:10) — the election is known through the calling.

Two guards keep this from going wrong. Their faith and love are not the ground of their election — that lies wholly in God — but they are the evidence of it; fruit confirming a root nobody can dig up and inspect. And notice the pastoral use Paul makes of the doctrine. He does not deploy it to sort the congregation or to threaten. He hands it to persecuted people as the one piece of ground that cannot shift: if your standing rested on the firmness of your own decision, a hard enough season could undo it; resting on his choice, it cannot.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Thessalonica was the provincial capital, and its religion was civic rather than private. Trade guilds met at sacrificial meals under patron gods; households kept their own deities; loyalty to Rome was expressed in the imperial cult. To turn from idols was not a change of opinion but resignation from the life of the town, which is precisely why affliction followed (v.6). And the whole thing happened fast: Paul had perhaps a month in the city (Acts 17:2) before a mob forced him out at night, yet within months this church was the pattern held up to older congregations across two provinces.

Now: Verse 3 supplies a test worth running, because faith, love and hope cost nothing to claim. Paul measures each by its output — work, exhaustion, staying put. Ask not whether you have them but whether anything in your week would look different if you did not. And verse 9 gives the useful form of the idol question: since ours are rarely carved, asking whether you own any statues settles nothing. Ask what you serve — what the week is organised around, what you are most afraid of losing, what you would trade sleep and integrity to keep.

verseByVerse.quote: We give thanks to God always for all of you, constantly mentioning you in our prayers,
verseByVerse.commentary:
We give thanks to God always for all of you, constantly mentioning you in our prayers,

We give thanks to God always for all of you. Three words govern this verse and each carries weight: always, all, constantly. Paul had left this church in the worst possible circumstances and had spent the intervening months, as chapter 3 will tell us, unable to bear the suspense and half-convinced his labour had been wasted. Thanksgiving was not his obvious response to Thessalonica. It was his settled one. And the thanks goes to God, not to the Thessalonians. Paul does not congratulate them on their faith. He thanks God for it, because their faith is God’s work.

For all of you. Not for the promising ones, or the ones who had held up best under pressure. All. Paul writes elsewhere to churches he has to correct sharply, and even there he usually thanks God for the whole body before he says anything else. Nobody is left out of his thanksgiving, because nobody in the church is there by his own achievement.

Constantly mentioning you in our prayers. The word means unceasingly, without a gap, and Paul uses it three times in this short letter (1:2; 2:13; 5:17), more than anywhere else he writes. He is describing a habit, not a mood: this church came up every time he prayed, specifically and by name, because he could not stop thinking about them.

What Paul did with his worry. There is a plain lesson here that most of us need more than we need a new doctrine. Paul is worried sick about these people and cannot reach them. What he does with the worry is turn it into thanksgiving and intercession. He does not brood, and he does not wait until the news is good. Anxiety about people you love is raw material, and Paul shows you what to do with it: carry it to God, and begin with what God has already done in them.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul prayed every second of the day. It means regular, faithful, persevering prayer, a standing habit of bringing these people before God.

How can I pray for people constantly when the list keeps growing? Pray regularly rather than exhaustively. Many Christians keep a short list for each day of the week, so that everyone comes round in turn, and then pray as people come to mind during the day, in a sentence, at the sink or on the bus. Begin, as Paul does, with thanks for what God has done in them, then ask for what they need. You will not pray for everyone every day, and you do not need to. What matters is that the people God has given you are not forgotten before him.

Why thank God, and not the person? Because faith, love and hope are gifts before they are achievements. It is right to encourage people, and Paul does so warmly in this very letter. But when you thank God for a brother’s faith, you are telling the truth about where it came from, and you keep both of you from pride.

In a sentence. We always thank God for all of you and continually mention you in our prayers.

On a Tuesday. Name three believers you know, especially one who worries you, and thank God for something specific he has done in each of them. Then ask him for what they need. Do it again tomorrow, and you will have begun Paul’s habit.

For worship. Thanks be to the God who makes faith where there was none, and keeps it alive in a hostile city when the apostle has been driven away. He is the one Paul thanked, and he is still the one at work in every believer you know. Their faith is his doing, and it is marvellous in our eyes.

verseByVerse.quote: remembering before our God and Father your work of faith and labor of love and steadfastness of hope in our Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
remembering before our God and Father your work of faith and labor of love and steadfastness of hope in our Lord Jesus Christ.

Remembering before our God and Father. In prayer Paul recalls what God has done in them, and here is the triad that will become famous, faith, love and hope, very likely the first time it was ever written down. But look at what Paul attaches to each, because the nouns are doing the real work: the work of faith, the labour of love, the steadfastness of hope.

Your work of faith. Faith produces work. Not work that earns anything (Paul will spend Romans and Galatians demolishing that idea), but work that faith itself generates, as a live root pushes up a shoot (Galatians 5:6; James 2:18). A faith that has changed nothing about what you do is a faith Paul would not recognise.

And labour of love. Love produces labour. The word is kopos, and it is not light work. It means toil to the point of weariness, the sweat of a man at the end of a long day. Paul does not say love produces warm feeling. He says it produces the kind of tiredness you get from doing something hard for somebody else. Most real love in a church looks like being worn out by people: the meals cooked, the hospital visits, the long conversation with someone who keeps returning to the same grief.

And steadfastness of hope. Hope produces steadfastness. The word is hypomonē, not passive resignation but the quality of a man who stays under a weight without buckling. And note the direction: hope is what makes endurance possible, not the other way round. You can bear almost anything if you know it ends, and how. These people were being persecuted; Paul tells them their staying power is fed by what is coming, the return of Christ.

In our Lord Jesus Christ. The phrase governs the whole line. This is not a list of admirable human qualities; it is a description of what Christ produces in people joined to him. Faith looks back to what Christ has done, love looks around to others for his sake, and hope looks forward to his coming. Paul returns to the three again and again (5:8; 1 Corinthians 13:13; Colossians 1:4–5), and in every place they are held together by the one person they look to.

What it does not mean. It does not mean works earn salvation. They are the work that faith produces, the fruit of a life God has already made new, never the price of his favour.

Is the work of faith the same as the works Paul rejects in Galatians? No. The works Paul rejects are works done to earn a right standing with God, as though our obedience could pay for acceptance. The work of faith is what faith does after God has freely accepted us in Christ: it trusts him, and so it obeys him, serves, forgives, and keeps going. The first is a wage; the second is a fruit. A Christian works hard, but from acceptance, not for it.

What if my love feels more like exhaustion than affection? Then you may be closer to this verse than you think. Paul chose the word for weary toil, not the word for warm feelings. Being tired from loving people is often a sign that love is real. But exhaustion also needs care: rest, prayer, and other believers sharing the load. Love that labours must also keep drawing from Christ, or it will curdle into resentment. Ask him for strength, and ask the church for help.

A test from the verse. Faith, love and hope are easy words and cost nothing to claim. Paul measures them by what they produce: work, weariness, staying put. Ask not whether you have them but whether anything in your week would be different if you did not.

In a sentence. We remember before our God and Father your work produced by faith, your labour prompted by love, and your endurance inspired by hope in our Lord Jesus Christ.

On a Tuesday. Take the week in front of you and look for the three. Where will faith have to act today, in a decision you would avoid if you did not trust God? Where will love cost you effort for someone else? Where will hope have to hold you steady under something you cannot change? Ask God to strengthen all three, and then do the work.

For worship. Glory to the Lord Jesus Christ, who is the root of all three. He is the one faith trusts, the one love serves, the one hope waits for. He makes weak people work, tired people love, and frightened people stand, and when the work is done, the labour spent and the waiting over, he himself will be the reward.
verseByVerse.note: Faith, love and hope — the triad Paul returns to again and again.

verseByVerse.quote: For we know, brothers loved by God, that he has chosen you,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For we know, brothers loved by God, that he has chosen you,

For we know, brothers loved by God. Two enormous things are said here almost in passing, and Paul says them to a church perhaps six months old. First: brothers loved by God. The word (ēgapēmenoi) is a perfect passive participle: having been loved, and standing loved. It is not a description of how God feels about them on a good day. It is a settled state they are in. And the ground of their election is that love, not anything in them (Deuteronomy 7:7–8; Ephesians 1:4–5). The word brothers, used here of the whole church, men and women together, is itself a gift: people who had lost their families by turning from the gods are told they have a new one.

That he has chosen you. The word is election (eklogē), the choosing out of some, and Paul states it flatly, without hedging or apology, as a comfort rather than a puzzle (2 Thessalonians 2:13). This is the doctrine some Christians find cold, and see where Paul puts it: in a letter to frightened people under persecution, as the first solid ground he can give them. If their standing rested on their own decision, a bad enough month could undo it. If it rests on his choice, it cannot.

How could Paul know? This is the question people ask in the car park afterwards. Election is a decree made in eternity, and no one has read the register. Paul is not claiming a private revelation. He tells us his evidence in the next word, because, and it runs straight into verse 5: he knows they were chosen because of how the gospel arrived among them and what it did when it arrived.

Where Christians differ: can we know who is elect? Some say election is unknowable and therefore irrelevant; others claim to know others’ eternal destiny. Some Christians also hold that God chose those he foresaw would believe. But Paul knows they were chosen because the gospel came to them in power and in the Holy Spirit (v. 5) and they received it: their faith is the evidence of God’s choice, not its cause. Verdict: Election is God’s free choice before the foundation of the world, not based on foreseen faith (Ephesians 1:4; Romans 9:11). We cannot read God’s secret will directly, but election shows itself in its fruits: the gospel received with power and conviction, a turning from idols, faith, love and hope (vv. 3–10; 2 Peter 1:10). So believers may have assurance of their election, and the church may speak of believers as chosen, while leaving final judgement to God (Westminster 3.8).

The pastoral shape of the doctrine. This is the answer to the person who lies awake wondering whether he is one of them. You do not find out by trying to read God’s mind. You look for the effects: a word that landed with power, a life that turned, a love for people you did not use to love, a persistence you cannot account for in yourself. The election is known through the calling (2 Peter 1:10). The root is hidden; the fruit is not. And note the tone. Paul does not use election to sort the congregation into sheep and goats, and he does not brandish it as a threat. He uses it the way you would use a deed of title with a nervous tenant: this is yours, and here is why nobody can take it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean election makes evangelism unnecessary. Election came to the Thessalonians through preaching (v. 5). God chose the people, and he also chose the means: a beaten missionary reasoning in a synagogue for three Sabbaths.

I cannot see much fruit in my life. Does that mean I am not chosen? Look more carefully, and look at the right things. The fruit is not spiritual brilliance but the marks Paul lists: you have heard the gospel and believe it is true; you have turned, however falteringly, from what you once served; you love God’s people and want to be with them; you keep coming back to Christ when you fail. Weak faith in Christ is still faith in Christ. And remember that assurance is not first found by staring inward. Look to Christ, who invites everyone who comes to him and casts out none (John 6:37). Whoever comes is chosen; election is God’s explanation of why you came.

If God has chosen, why should I pray for unbelievers or share the gospel? Because God has chosen to save his people through prayer and preaching, and he gives us the privilege of being his means. Election is the reason evangelism is hopeful, not the reason it is pointless. Paul went to Corinth knowing that God had many people in that city (Acts 18:10), and the knowledge kept him preaching for eighteen months. We do not know who the elect are, so we tell everyone, and we pray expecting God to open hearts.

In a sentence. For we know, brothers and sisters loved by God, that he has chosen you,

On a Tuesday. When your standing with God feels fragile, after a bad week, a sharp temptation, a cold season in prayer, do not build your assurance on how you feel today. Rehearse the facts: God loved you before you loved him; he chose you before you chose him; his choice is the ground, and your faith is the fruit. Then look for the fruit honestly, and thank him for every trace of it.

For worship. Before the world was made, God set his love on people who would one day bow to idols in a Greek port, and he did not change his mind when they did. In the fullness of time he sent his Son to die for them, and then a tired missionary to tell them, and the Spirit to open their ears. If you are in Christ, the same love chose you. Nothing in you started it, and nothing in you will end it. Bow in wonder, and give him the glory.

verseByVerse.quote: because our gospel came to you not only in word, but also in power and in the Holy Spirit and with full conviction. You know what kind of men we proved to be among you for your sake.
verseByVerse.commentary:
because our gospel came to you not only in word, but also in power and in the Holy Spirit and with full conviction. You know what kind of men we proved to be among you for your sake.

Because our gospel came to you not only in word. Here is Paul’s evidence, and it has two halves. The gospel came to them in word: it was preached, it had content, it was argued from the Scriptures for three Sabbaths, and there is no gospel without words. But not only in word.

But also in power and in the Holy Spirit. Words are the instrument; they are not the agent. Paul was as capable a speaker as the early church had, and he refuses to credit the result to his own delivery. The Spirit made the words effective and changed hearts (Romans 1:16; 1 Corinthians 2:4). The same sermon can be preached twice and leave one room unmoved and another in tears, and the difference is not the sermon.

And with full conviction. The word is plērophoria, a word for something carried all the way to completion: settled, unhesitating certainty. It probably covers both sides of the event. The preachers spoke with full assurance, and the hearers received it with full assurance. Not that they found the argument persuasive, though it was. The thing landed on them with the weight of fact.

You know what kind of men we proved to be among you for your sake. This is the half of the verse most often skipped. Paul does not stop at the Spirit’s power; he points to the messengers themselves, and to what these people had watched with their own eyes. What had they watched? Men who arrived with their backs still marked from a flogging in Philippi (2:2), who worked night and day at a trade so as not to burden anybody (2:9), and who left town under cover of darkness rather than get their converts killed. The gospel did not come to Thessalonica as a lecture. It came in the hands of men whose lives corroborated it, and Paul says so, for your sake, because even that was aimed at them, not at his own reputation. He will defend his conduct at length in chapter 2.

How the gospel travels. Hold the two halves together and you have Paul’s whole account of how the gospel travels. The Spirit gives the power; a life gives the credibility. Neither substitutes for the other. A blameless life without the word saves nobody, and the word from a life that contradicts it will be weighed and dismissed, and rightly.

What it does not mean. It does not mean words are unimportant. The Spirit works through the word, not apart from it. Power and the Holy Spirit came with the gospel, not instead of it.

Does power mean miracles? Should we expect them when we preach? Paul may include the signs that accompanied the apostles’ ministry (Romans 15:19; 2 Corinthians 12:12), but his main point is the power that converts: the Spirit opening blind eyes to the truth of Christ. The app’s view is cessationist, held charitably: the miraculous sign-gifts that authenticated the apostles and their message belonged to that founding period, while the Spirit’s converting power goes on in every age. So yes, expect power when the gospel is preached, the greatest power there is: dead hearts made alive. That is a greater wonder than a healed body, and God still does it.

I am not a preacher. Does this verse apply to me? Yes. Every Christian who speaks of Christ to a friend, a child or a colleague does what Paul did on a smaller scale: speaks true words, depending on the Spirit to make them live, from a life that does not contradict them. You cannot supply the power, and you are not asked to. You are asked to say what is true, kindly and clearly, and to live so that your words are believable.

In a sentence. because our gospel came to you not simply with words but also with power, with the Holy Spirit and deep conviction. You know how we lived among you for your sake.

On a Tuesday. Before you speak to anyone about Christ, pray that the Spirit will make your words powerful, because they will not be powerful otherwise. Then look at your life from the outside, as a neighbour sees it: your temper, your honesty at work, your money, the way you speak of others. Ask whether it backs up your words or undercuts them, and bring what undercuts them to God.

For worship. Praise to the Holy Spirit, who takes ordinary words from ordinary mouths and makes them the voice of God to a dead heart. He did it in a Thessalonian synagogue and a Thessalonian workshop, and he does it still. The preacher cannot convert anyone; the Spirit converts multitudes. Every believer is a monument to his power, and every one of them first heard Christ in words.

verseByVerse.quote: And you became imitators of us and of the Lord, for you received the word in much affliction, with the joy of the Holy Spirit, so that you became an example to all the believers in Macedonia and in Achaia.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And you became imitators of us and of the Lord, for you received the word in much affliction, with the joy of the Holy Spirit, so that you became an example to all the believers in Macedonia and in Achaia.

And you became imitators of us and of the Lord. They copied the missionaries, and through them the Lord himself, and Paul immediately says in what respect, because otherwise the claim is impossibly vague. They imitated him in this: you received the word in much affliction, with the joy of the Holy Spirit. That is the point of resemblance. Not Paul’s gifts, not his knowledge: the way he took a beating and kept his joy. And behind Paul stands the Lord, who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross (Hebrews 12:2).

They had seen him do it. These people had watched Paul arrive with his back marked from Philippi and preach anyway; some of them had watched him hustled out of town at night. Then the same trouble came on them, and they behaved the same way. Imitation in the New Testament is rarely about copying a technique. It is about having watched somebody under pressure and finding, when your turn comes, that you do what they did.

For you received the word in much affliction. The word is thlipsis, pressure, the crushing weight. They believed in the middle of riots and opposition (Acts 17:5–9), and as chapter 2 will show, their own countrymen turned on them (2:14). This was real trouble, not inconvenience.

With the joy of the Holy Spirit. Note whose joy it is. Not joy they worked up, and not the absence of pain, but something the Spirit produced in them while the pressure was still on, a supernatural joy that persecution could not destroy (Acts 13:52). Hold the two halves of the phrase together, because either one alone is a different religion. Affliction without joy is simply misfortune and nobody remarks on it. Joy without affliction is cheap and proves nothing. Joy inside affliction is a fact that demands an explanation, and people go looking for one.

So that you became an example to all the believers in Macedonia and in Achaia. The word is typos: the mark left by a blow, a die, a stamp; our word type. They had been struck by the gospel and now carried its impression, and other churches could read it off them. Macedonia was the northern province, including Philippi and Beroea; Achaia was the Roman province of southern Greece, with Athens and Corinth its chief cities.

Weigh how quickly this happened. Paul had been with them a matter of weeks. He is writing months later, and already this congregation of new converts is the pattern held up to the churches of two Roman provinces. Length of time in the faith and usefulness to God are not the same measurement.

What it does not mean. It does not mean joy means the absence of sorrow. It means joy deeper than circumstances, a gladness in God that lives alongside tears without being drowned by them (2 Corinthians 6:10).

Is it wrong to feel sad or afraid when I suffer? No. The Lord Jesus wept and was troubled in spirit, and Paul himself writes of grief and anxiety in this letter (2:17; 3:5). The joy of the Spirit is not a fixed smile or a denial of pain. It is a deeper gladness that Christ is yours and that nothing can take him from you, a joy that can sit beside sorrow and outlast it. If you cannot feel it today, ask for it; it is the Spirit’s gift, not your achievement.

Is it right to imitate human leaders? Yes, so far as they imitate Christ (1 Corinthians 11:1). Paul deliberately offered his life as a pattern, and God gives his church living examples because we learn best by watching. But the imitation always passes through the man to the Lord. Copy a Christian’s faith, patience and love; never make him your master, and never follow him where he departs from Christ.

In a sentence. You became imitators of us and of the Lord, for you welcomed the message in the midst of severe suffering with the joy given by the Holy Spirit. And so you became a model to all the believers in Macedonia and Achaia.

On a Tuesday. Think of one believer you have watched suffer well, and ask what exactly you saw: what they said, what they refused to say, where they went for help. Then ask who might be watching you in your present difficulty. You are teaching someone how a Christian carries trouble, whether you mean to or not. Ask the Holy Spirit for joy in the middle of it.

For worship. Blessed be the Spirit who puts joy where the world can only see loss. Blessed be the Lord Jesus, who walked into affliction for the joy set before him and makes his people able to follow. And blessed be the God who took a few weeks of preaching and a few months of persecution and stamped the image of his Son on a whole church.
verseByVerse.note: Achaia was the Roman province of southern Greece, with Corinth as its capital.

verseByVerse.quote: For not only has the word of the Lord sounded forth from you in Macedonia and Achaia, but your faith in God has gone forth everywhere, so that we need not say anything.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For not only has the word of the Lord sounded forth from you in Macedonia and Achaia, but your faith in God has gone forth everywhere, so that we need not say anything.

For not only has the word of the Lord sounded forth from you. The verb is the striking thing: exēcheō, from which we get echo. It is used of a trumpet blast and of thunder rolling out. The picture is not of missionaries dispatched but of a sound that carries: the gospel struck this church like a hammer on a bell, and the ringing went out across the province. And the tense is perfect: it sounded and is still sounding. Paul is not describing a campaign that finished. He is describing a noise that has not yet stopped.

In Macedonia and Achaia, but your faith in God has gone forth everywhere. Thessalonica sat on the Via Egnatia and was a busy port. Travellers, traders and sailors passed through constantly, and they carried the story with them. The church did not organise this. They simply lived in a city everybody went through, and what could be seen of them was worth repeating. Changed lives are the best advertisement the gospel has.

So that we need not say anything. A line with a smile in it. Paul, whose entire vocation was saying things, arrives somewhere to talk about the gospel and finds the ground already covered. People tell him about the Thessalonians before he can tell them. He is delighted to be redundant.

What actually travelled. There is something bracing here for ordinary Christians who feel they have no gift for evangelism. What travelled was not a programme or an argument. It was a report: that a group of people in Thessalonica had dropped their idols and would not stop being glad about it under pressure. Nobody in that church set out to be famous across two provinces. They were simply visible.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every person in the world had heard. Everywhere is the natural exaggeration of delight: it means their reputation had spread widely, far beyond where Paul could have taken it.

Does every Christian have to evangelise? I am shy and not good with words. Every Christian is a witness, but not every Christian is a preacher. The Thessalonians spread the word first by being a visible, changed people, and then by speaking when people asked about it (1 Peter 3:15). You can do both. Live openly as a Christian, let people know you go to church and why, pray for the people around you, invite them to hear the gospel, and when someone asks why you have hope, tell them simply what Christ has done for you. The Lord uses quiet voices. Faithfulness, not eloquence, is what he asks.

Is the word of the Lord the Bible, or the spoken gospel? Here it is the gospel message about Christ, spoken and passed on. That message is the same word God has now given us, fixed and complete, in Scripture. What sounded out from Thessalonica was not new revelation from the church but the apostolic gospel the church had received, repeated faithfully.

In a sentence. The Lord’s message rang out from you not only in Macedonia and Achaia; your faith in God has become known everywhere. Therefore we do not need to say anything about it,

On a Tuesday. Every church has a reputation in its town, and it is never the one printed on the noticeboard. It is whatever the neighbours say when the subject comes up. Ask what is sounding forth from yours, and from you: at work, in the street, in your family. Let your faith be the kind others talk about, not for your glory, but so the word of the Lord rings out.

For worship. The word of the Lord is a living thing. It struck a little church in a port city and the sound went round the world, and it has not stopped ringing, for it has reached you. Praise to the God whose word does not return to him empty (Isaiah 55:11), who spreads the fame of his Son through ordinary people who were simply seen to be glad.

verseByVerse.quote: For they themselves report concerning us the kind of reception we had among you, and how you turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For they themselves report concerning us the kind of reception we had among you, and how you turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God,

For they themselves report concerning us the kind of reception we had among you. Paul now quotes what other people are saying about the missionaries’ visit, and it turns out to be one of the most compact summaries of conversion in the New Testament. Two movements: a turning to, and a turning from.

And how you turned to God from idols. Note the order in which Paul reports it: toward God first, and from idols as the consequence. That is nearly always the actual sequence. People rarely put down an idol because they have been persuaded it is worthless in the abstract; they put it down because something better has taken hold of them. Try to reverse it and you get willpower, which is a short-lived fuel. The turning was decisive, a conversion, not a rearrangement. And the phrase from idols tells us that most of this church were converted pagans, not Jews.

What it cost in that city. Thessalonica was the provincial capital, thick with the worship of Dionysus, Serapis and the Cabiri, and, most dangerously, with the cult of the emperor. Religion there was not a private preference. It was civic membership: the trade guilds had patron gods and their meetings were sacrificial meals, family life ran on household deities, and public loyalty was measured by attendance. To turn from idols was to resign from the life of the town. It explains the affliction of verse 6 entirely.

To serve the living and true God. Both adjectives are aimed. An idol is not living: it is wood and stone, and Isaiah mocked the man who fells a tree, burns half of it to warm himself and worships the other half (Isaiah 44:14–17). And it is not true: it does not correspond to anything. Paul is using the language of Jeremiah, who called the LORD the true God and the living God (Jeremiah 10:10) against exactly such rivals (Acts 14:15).

Serve. The verb is douleuō, to serve as a slave. That is a blunt word for what they turned to, and it is deliberate. They did not exchange servitude for independence. They changed owners. The question a person faces is never whether to serve something but which master is worth it, and only one of the available masters is alive. Only one of them died for his servants.

What it does not mean. It does not mean modern people have no idols. Anything we trust, love or fear more than God is an idol (Colossians 3:5), whether or not it has a shrine.

How do I find my idols if I own no statues? Asking whether you own any statues settles nothing. Ask instead what you serve: what you organise your week around, what you are afraid of losing, what you daydream about, what you would sacrifice sleep, money and integrity to keep, and what makes you angry or despairing when it is threatened. Good things become idols when we ask them to give us what only God can give: security, worth, comfort, control. That is the altar, whatever is or is not standing on it.

How do I actually turn from an idol? The same way the Thessalonians did: by turning to God first. Confess it to him by name. Then look hard at the living and true God, his goodness, his promises, his Son, until the idol looks small beside him. Cut off what feeds it where you can, and replace it with service: give away some of the money, use the time for others, bring the fear to God in prayer every time it rises. Expect to turn again and again. Old idols rarely leave in one day, but a heart that has seen the living God never fully goes back.

In a sentence. for they themselves report what kind of reception you gave us. They tell how you turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God,

On a Tuesday. Name one thing that competes with God for your heart, the thing you look to when you are anxious or bored or hurt. Tell God about it honestly. Then do one concrete act today that serves him instead of it, and thank him for the living and true God you now serve.

For worship. The idols of Thessalonica are dust, and the God the Thessalonians turned to is as alive as on the day they first heard of him. He is living, and he gives life; he is true, and he never deceives. He is the only master who has ever bought his servants with his own blood, and his service is perfect freedom. Glory to the living and true God.
verseByVerse.note: Turning “from idols” shows that most of the church were converted pagans, not Jews.

verseByVerse.quote: and to wait for his Son from heaven, whom he raised from the dead, Jesus who delivers us from the wrath to come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and to wait for his Son from heaven, whom he raised from the dead, Jesus who delivers us from the wrath to come.

And to wait for his Son from heaven. The report has one more clause, and it shapes the rest of the letter. Two verbs describe the Christian life here: to serve, and to wait. Work and watch, neither without the other. The waiting (anamenō) is not idleness; the word carries expectancy, like watching a road for someone you love. And remember how new these believers were. Within weeks of conversion they had been taught to live with their eyes on the horizon, so much so that by chapter 4 they are anxious about what happens to those who die before he arrives. The second coming runs through every chapter of this letter (2:19; 3:13; 4:13–18; 5:1–11, 23).

Whom he raised from the dead. Here are the grounds for expecting him at all. The return is not a hope hanging in mid-air. It rests on something that has already happened in public. The resurrection proves he is God’s Son and guarantees his return as Judge (Acts 17:31; Romans 1:4). A man who has been raised is a man who can come back.

Jesus who delivers us from the wrath to come. This clause needs handling with care. Modern readers flinch at wrath, often because they picture divine temper, God losing control. That is not the biblical idea. God’s wrath is his settled, just opposition to evil, and a God who felt nothing about cruelty and injustice would not be good. We would not admire a judge who shrugged at atrocity. The wrath to come is God’s judgement on sin at the end (Romans 2:5; 5:9), the guarantee that the accounts of history will finally be settled.

The tense is the comfort. Paul does not tell frightened, persecuted people that wrath is coming for them. He tells them the opposite. Jesus delivers (rhyomai, rescues), and the participle is present: a rescue already in force. The wrath is future; the deliverance is a fact now. They are not hoping to escape. They have been taken out already, by the one who absorbed it himself, bearing in his own body on the cross the judgement his people deserved.

Where Christians differ: wrath and the rapture. Some read deliverance from the wrath to come (here and 5:9) as a promise that believers will be removed from the earth in a secret rapture before a seven-year tribulation. Verdict: The wrath to come is God’s final judgement on the ungodly at the last day (Romans 2:5; 2 Thessalonians 1:7–9). Believers are rescued from it through Christ’s death and resurrection. This does not promise escape from all suffering beforehand; the Thessalonians were already suffering (v. 6; 3:3). Christ will return once, visibly, to raise the dead, rescue his people and judge the world. There is no secret rapture.

What it does not mean. It does not mean waiting is passive. They waited by serving (v. 9).

Why would a loving God have wrath at all? Because love that does not oppose evil is not love. A father who felt nothing when his child was abused would not be loving; he would be indifferent. God’s wrath is the resistance of his holiness and love to everything that destroys what he made. The wonder of the gospel is not that God has no wrath, but that he himself, in his Son, bore it for us, so that his justice and his mercy meet at the cross (Romans 3:25–26).

I still sin. Am I really safe from the wrath to come? Yes, if you are in Christ. Your rescue does not rest on how well you have done this week but on what Jesus did once for all and on his present work for you. The wrath your sins deserve fell on him; there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). Your continuing sin should grieve you and drive you back to him, but it cannot reopen a case he has closed. He delivers, present tense: he is still doing it.

Does waiting for Jesus mean I should try to work out when he will come? No. Jesus said no one knows the day or hour (Matthew 24:36), and Paul will say the day comes like a thief (5:2). Waiting means living ready, not calculating dates. It means holding this world loosely, serving faithfully where you are, and being glad, not afraid, at the thought that he might come today.

A whole life in ten verses. The chapter that began with three men and a greeting ends looking down the road. Turned, serving, waiting: past, present and future, the whole Christian life inside ten verses, and Jesus at both ends of it, the one who was raised and the one who is coming.

In a sentence. and to wait for his Son from heaven, whom he raised from the dead: Jesus, who rescues us from the coming wrath.

On a Tuesday. Live today as someone waiting for Jesus from heaven. Ask what you would want him to find you doing if he came this afternoon, and then do it: serve while you wait. When fear of judgement rises, answer it with the present tense of this verse: Jesus delivers me.

For worship. Glory to the Son who came down from heaven to bear the wrath, who was raised from the dead by the Father, and who will come again from heaven to bring his people home. The wrath to come is real, and he stood under all of it for us. Now we wait for him, not as criminals for a judge but as a bride for her husband, and the one we wait for is Jesus, our Deliverer.
