3.title: Standing Firm in the Lord
3.overview:
Paul could not bear not knowing whether the young church had survived persecution. So he stayed alone in Athens and sent Timothy back to strengthen them, reminding them that suffering was what they had been warned to expect, and fearing that the tempter had talked them out of the faith. Now Timothy has returned with good news: their faith and love are holding, and they long to see Paul as he longs to see them.

Paul says, “now we live, if you are standing fast in the Lord.” He cannot thank God enough, and prays night and day to see them and fill the gaps in their teaching. The chapter ends with a prayer that God will clear his road to them, make their love overflow to everyone, and strengthen their hearts to be blameless in holiness when Jesus comes with all his holy ones.

verseByVerse.ref: 3:1–5 – Timothy Sent, and Suffering as a Posting
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Unable to bear the silence any longer, Paul stayed alone in Athens and sent Timothy, his fellow worker, to strengthen and encourage them, so that no one would be shaken by their troubles. Paul had warned them that suffering was part of the Christian calling, and it had come. He sent Timothy for fear that the tempter had shaken their faith and his work had been wasted.
verseByVerse.theology:
Affliction as Appointment, Not Accident

The key word in verse 3 is keimetha — we are laid, set in place, appointed. It is the language of a stone set in a foundation or a sentry posted, and Paul uses the same root of himself in prison, put there for the defence of the gospel (Phil 1:16). Suffering for the gospel is not something that slipped past God's attention; it is a placement.

That is the pastoral logic, and it needs stating carefully. What steadies a shaken believer is not the promise that the trouble will stop but the assurance that the trouble is not a mistake. If hardship means the plan has gone wrong, every difficult week is evidence against the faith. If hardship is where God has laid you, the difficult week proves only that you are where he put you. The Reformed tradition has held this consistently: God governs all things, his people's afflictions included, and such suffering is purposeful — producing endurance, character and hope (Rom 5:3-4).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul feared not that persecution would smash this church but that it would coax them out of it (v.3) — faith is usually lost by erosion, not by renunciation.

Now: Honest preparation for hardship is a form of pastoral care, and its absence is a cruelty disguised as encouragement (v.4).

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore when we could bear it no longer, we were willing to be left behind at Athens alone, and we sent Timothy, our brother and God's coworker in the gospel of Christ, to establish and exhort you in your faith,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore when we could bear it no longer, we were willing to be left behind at Athens alone, and we sent Timothy, our brother and God’s coworker in the gospel of Christ, to establish and exhort you in your faith,

Meaning first. 1 Thessalonians 3 shows a pastor’s heart in anxiety and relief. Unable to bear not knowing how the young church was doing under persecution, Paul stayed alone in Athens and sent Timothy to strengthen them, reminding them that suffering was to be expected and fearing that the tempter had shaken them (vv. 1–5). Then Timothy returned with wonderful news of their faith and love and their longing to see Paul. Paul was comforted in his own troubles: now we really live, if you stand firm in the Lord (vv. 6–8). He overflows with thanks and prays night and day to see them again and supply what is lacking in their faith (vv. 9–10). The chapter ends with a prayer: that God would open the way for Paul to come, make their love increase, and establish their hearts blameless in holiness at the coming of the Lord Jesus with all his saints (vv. 11–13). Behind the human drama stands the God who keeps his people when their pastor cannot reach them.

Therefore when we could bear it no longer. The verb is stegō, and it means to cover, to keep water out, to hold something in; it is used of a roof and of a watertight vessel. Paul had been containing his anxiety about this church, and the seams gave way. He says it twice in five verses (vv. 1, 5), which is not a man choosing a phrase but a man telling you what the months had been like.

We were willing to be left behind at Athens alone. Then what he did about it, and the cost is easy to miss. Paul had gone from Beroea to Athens (Acts 17:15–34). Read Acts 17 for what that meant. Athens was where Paul’s spirit was provoked within him at a city full of idols, where he was brought before the Areopagus, mocked when he mentioned resurrection, and where he made few converts: the thinnest ground he ever worked. He was in that city, and he gave away his companion. The word for left behind (kataleipō) is used elsewhere of being abandoned, and alone sits at the end of the clause, carrying its weight. Paul was not a man who liked working alone; his letters are full of names. He chose isolation in a hostile city because a frightened congregation far away needed someone more than he did. That is the whole argument of the previous chapter, sharing not only the gospel but our own selves, happening in an actual decision with an actual price.

And we sent Timothy, our brother and God’s coworker in the gospel of Christ. Notice he does not call him his assistant. God’s coworker: a startling title for a young man, and one Paul does not soften. Some manuscripts read God’s servant, as the ESV notes, and the variation probably arose because copyists found the bolder title surprising. The work of steadying a church is God’s work, and the person doing it is working alongside God, not running errands for an apostle.

To establish and exhort you in your faith. Timothy’s brief has two verbs. To establish them (stērizō): the word means to make firm, to prop or buttress, what you do to a wall that is leaning. And to exhort them (parakaleō): to come alongside and urge. Roots and backbone. Notice that both are about stability rather than growth; when a church is under attack the first task is not advancement but keeping it standing. New believers need follow-up care, and God provides it through people.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul doubted God. He knew new believers under pressure need support, and he knew God gives that support through means.

If God keeps his people, why was Paul so anxious? Because God keeps his people through means, and Paul was one of the means. Trusting God’s sovereignty never made Paul passive; it made him pray and send. His anxiety was the anxiety of love, not of unbelief, and he did with it what love should do: he acted, and he brought it to God. Your concern for a struggling believer is not a lack of faith. It may be God’s way of moving you to be the help he intends.

What does following up a new believer actually involve? What Timothy did: going to them, strengthening their grasp of the truth, encouraging them to keep going, and preparing them for trouble. In practice that means meeting regularly, reading the Bible together, answering questions, praying with them, introducing them to other believers, and noticing when they go quiet. It does not require a title. It requires time, patience and love, and it is some of the most fruitful work in the church.

In a sentence. So when we could stand it no longer, we thought it best to be left by ourselves in Athens. We sent Timothy, who is our brother and co-worker in God’s service in spreading the gospel of Christ, to strengthen and encourage you in your faith,

On a Tuesday. Think of a young or struggling believer you know, someone new to faith or wobbling under pressure. Go, call or write this week. Ask how they are, open the Bible with them if you can, and pray with them. You will be doing God’s work alongside him.

For worship. The God who sent Timothy to Thessalonica is the God who sent his Son to us. He does not leave his people to stand alone; he props up leaning walls and steadies trembling hearts. And he has made ordinary believers his coworkers, which is the greatest honour a human being can receive. Glory to the God who establishes his church.

verseByVerse.quote: that no one be moved by these afflictions. For you yourselves know that we are destined for this.
verseByVerse.commentary:
that no one be moved by these afflictions. For you yourselves know that we are destined for this.

That no one be moved by these afflictions. Here is the reason for the whole mission. The verb is sainō, and it is an odd and vivid one. Its root use is of a dog wagging its tail: fawning, being coaxed. From there it came to mean being beguiled, shifted from your position by something that flatters or unsettles you. Paul’s worry is not only that persecution would smash them. It is subtler: that under sustained pressure they would be gently talked out of it, drift, be coaxed back to the life they left, or tempted to compromise to escape the pressure.

How faith is usually lost. That is usually how it happens. Not in a moment of dramatic renunciation, but by erosion: the family who keep asking, the invitation it is easier to accept, the guild dinner it costs too much to refuse. A wagging tail, not a battering ram.

For you yourselves know that we are destined for this. Against that Paul sets one fact. The verb is keimetha: we are laid, set in place, appointed. It is the same verb Paul used of himself in prison, put here for the defence of the gospel (Philippians 1:16), and it is used of a stone set in a foundation or a sentry posted. Affliction is not something that happened to slip past God’s attention. It is a placement (Acts 14:22; John 16:33; 2 Timothy 3:12).

The pastoral logic. Take the two halves together and you see it. The thing that steadies a shaken believer is not being told the trouble will stop. It is being told the trouble is not a mistake. If suffering means the plan has gone wrong, every hard week is evidence against the faith; if suffering is where God has laid you, then the hard week is not evidence of anything except that you are where he put you. Knowing this in advance protects from shock.

You yourselves know. Notice the small phrase. Paul is not breaking news. He had told them this in advance, which is the subject of the very next verse and one of the quiet marks of an honest ministry.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God delights in his people’s pain. It means he uses it for their good and his glory (Romans 8:28; 1 Peter 1:6–7).

Does destined for this apply to all suffering, or only persecution? Paul’s immediate subject is suffering for the gospel, the pressure that comes because you belong to Christ. But the principle reaches further: nothing comes to God’s children by accident, whether illness, loss or disappointment, and he works all of it for their good (Romans 8:28). That does not make every hardship good in itself, nor does it mean you must not seek relief. Pray for healing, seek justice, take the medicine. But you can do so knowing that you are where your Father has placed you, and that he has not lost track of you.

Is it wrong to try to avoid persecution? Not in itself. Jesus told his disciples to flee from one town to the next (Matthew 10:23), and Paul left Thessalonica and Damascus by night. What is wrong is avoiding it by denying Christ or compromising obedience. You may leave, keep a low profile in some settings, or use the law’s protection, as Paul used his citizenship. You may not lie about him, worship what he forbids, or abandon his people to save yourself.

In a sentence. so that no one would be unsettled by these trials. For you know quite well that we are destined for them.

On a Tuesday. Notice where you are being gently coaxed away from Christ: not attacked, just nudged. The joke you laugh along with, the habit you have quietly resumed, the conviction you no longer mention. Name it before God, and stand where he has placed you.

For worship. If you are suffering, it is not a sign God has forgotten you. The Father appointed suffering for his own Son before he appointed it for us, and through that suffering he brought many sons to glory. The road he lays for his children may be hard, but he walks it with them, and it ends at his throne. Blessed be the God whose appointments are never mistakes.

verseByVerse.quote: For when we were with you, we kept telling you beforehand that we were to suffer affliction, just as it has come to pass, and just as you know. For this reason, when I could bear it no longer, I sent to learn about your faith, for fear that somehow the tempter had tempted you and our labor would be in vain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For when we were with you, we kept telling you beforehand that we were to suffer affliction, just as it has come to pass, and just as you know. For this reason, when I could bear it no longer, I sent to learn about your faith, for fear that somehow the tempter had tempted you and our labor would be in vain.

For when we were with you, we kept telling you beforehand that we were to suffer affliction. The tense is continuous: he kept on telling them. This was not a footnote delivered once; it was part of the standing instruction, repeated in a stay of perhaps a month. Weigh what Paul chose to spend his limited time on. He had a few weeks with brand-new converts and an enormous amount he might have taught them. High on the list was: this will cost you, and here is what is coming. He did not win them with an easier offer and explain the terms later. Honest evangelism counts the cost (Luke 14:28).

Just as it has come to pass, and just as you know. The warning was verified by events, and that verification is itself pastoral. When the trouble arrived it did not arrive as a contradiction of what they had been taught but as a confirmation of it. A church told the truth in advance can meet hardship saying he said this would happen; a church promised an easy road meets the same hardship asking whether the whole thing was false.

For this reason, when I could bear it no longer, I sent to learn about your faith. Now the plural becomes singular: I. Paul admits his own fear, and he is not embarrassed by it.

For fear that somehow the tempter had tempted you. The tempter is the title used of Satan in the wilderness (Matthew 4:3), where the tactic was not violence but suggestion. Paul has already named him as the one who cut the road (2:18). He sees a strategy: block the teacher, then work on the church, using suffering to tempt believers to give up.

And our labour would be in vain. In vain is kenos again, the empty word from 2:1, where he insisted his coming had not been empty. Here is the honest underside of that confidence: he was genuinely afraid it might yet prove so. The apostle who writes so certainly about God’s election in chapter 1 also lay awake wondering whether his work in Thessalonica had come to nothing. Both are in the same short letter, and neither cancels the other.

Strong faith and real anxiety. Say that to anyone who assumes that strong faith means the absence of anxiety. Paul was sure of God and frightened about the outcome at the same time, and he did the only useful thing available: he could not go, so he sent, and then he waited.

What it does not mean. It does not mean true believers can be lost. Paul feared that their faith might prove false, which would show his labour fruitless. Timothy’s report proved it genuine.

If true believers cannot be lost, why did Paul fear? Because he could not see their hearts, only their outward profession, and he knew that some who make a start fall away because their faith was never real (Matthew 13:20–21; 1 John 2:19). God’s elect will persevere (John 10:28–29; Philippians 1:6), and they persevere by means: warnings, teaching, encouragement, prayer. Paul’s fear moved him to supply those means. So we hold both: unshakeable confidence in God’s keeping, and earnest care that no one drifts. The doctrine of perseverance is not a reason to stop watching over one another.

How do I tell people the cost without frightening them away? Tell them the truth with the reward in view. Jesus never hid the cost of discipleship, and he never mentioned it without the treasure: whoever loses his life for my sake will find it (Matthew 16:25). Say plainly that following Christ may cost friendships, comfort and reputation. Then say why it is worth it: forgiveness, adoption, a living hope, Christ himself. People who are told the truth are not easily shaken when the trouble comes.

In a sentence. In fact, when we were with you, we kept telling you that we would be persecuted. And it turned out that way, as you well know. For this reason, when Paul could stand it no longer, he sent to find out about your faith. He was afraid that in some way the tempter had tempted you and that our labours might have been in vain.

On a Tuesday. When you share the gospel, be honest about the cost as well as the gift. And think of someone under pressure to give up: pray for them by name today, that the tempter would not have his way, and send them a word of encouragement.

For worship. The Lord Jesus told his disciples the truth: in the world you will have tribulation. And then he said, take heart, I have overcome the world (John 16:33). The tempter came to him in the wilderness and was beaten, and he will not finally have any of Christ’s sheep. Our labour in the Lord is never in vain, because the Lord who keeps his people is faithful.

verseByVerse.ref: 3:6–13 – The News From Home, and a Prayer for Love
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Timothy has now come back with good news of their faith and love, and their warm memories and longing to see Paul. That news has comforted him in his own distress; it is like new life to him to know they stand firm in the Lord. He cannot thank God enough for the joy they bring him, and he prays earnestly to see them again and supply what their faith still lacks. He prays that God will open the way, that the Lord will make their love for one another and for everyone overflow, and that he will strengthen their hearts to be blameless in holiness before God at the coming of the Lord Jesus with all his holy ones.
verseByVerse.theology:
Two Persons, One Verb

In verse 11 Paul names the Father and the Lord Jesus as two subjects and gives them one singular verb — the highest view of Christ, already present in the ordinary shape of a man's prayers.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: What was lacking in their faith (v.10) was not sincerity but completeness — the teaching Paul never got to give.

Now: Paul prays that a persecuted church would overflow in love not only for one another but ‘for all’ (v.12) — the very population making its life hard.

verseByVerse.quote: But now that Timothy has come to us from you, and has brought us the good news of your faith and love and reported that you always remember us kindly and long to see us, as we long to see you— for this reason, brothers, in all our distress and affliction we have been comforted about you through your faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But now that Timothy has come to us from you, and has brought us the good news of your faith and love and reported that you always remember us kindly and long to see us, as we long to see you—for this reason, brothers, in all our distress and affliction we have been comforted about you through your faith.

But now that Timothy has come to us from you. You can feel the letter change temperature. Everything before this was the waiting; this is the news arriving. Timothy had rejoined Paul in Corinth (Acts 18:5), and this letter was written in the first glow of his report.

And has brought us the good news of your faith and love. The word Paul uses for what Timothy brought is the striking thing: euangelizomai, he gospelled us. It is the verb for preaching the good news, and this is the only place in all Paul’s letters where he uses it of anything other than the gospel of Christ. News that a church was standing firm was, to him, of the same order as the message itself: good news of God’s work in the world. Faith and love: their relationship to God, and to one another.

Three answers to three fears. Timothy’s report has three parts, each answering one of Paul’s fears. Their faith: they had not been coaxed away. Their love: the community had not turned on itself under pressure. And that you always remember us kindly and long to see us: they had not concluded that Paul abandoned them.

And reported that you always remember us kindly and long to see us, as we long to see you. That third item matters more than it looks. Paul had left in the night and never come back; his enemies had a ready-made accusation. He had been anxious not only about their faith but about whether they still thought well of him. The slanders had not turned them against him. Timothy’s news was that the affection ran both ways.

For this reason, brothers, in all our distress and affliction we have been comforted about you through your faith. Do not miss the direction. Paul is the apostle; they are the young converts; and it is their faith that comforts him. He was in Corinth by now, in his own trouble. He tells us he was there in weakness and fear and much trembling (1 Corinthians 2:3), and Acts records that the Lord had to tell him in a vision not to be afraid (Acts 18:9–10).

The traffic runs both ways. In a healthy church it is never one-way. The people who are supposed to be doing the strengthening are themselves held up by the perseverance of ordinary believers they are worried about. If you have ever wondered whether your quiet faithfulness matters to anyone, this verse is the answer: it was the thing that got Paul through Corinth.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul’s comfort depended only on them. It came from God, through them, as he says in the same way of Titus’s arrival: God, who comforts the downcast, comforted us (2 Corinthians 7:6).

Is it all right to care what people think of me? It is right to care about being loved by your brothers and sisters, and to be grieved when relationships are damaged by slander. Paul did. What is wrong is letting their opinion govern your obedience (2:4). Paul would have preached the same gospel whether they thought well of him or not, but he was glad, deeply, that they did. Love wants to be loved back, and that is not vanity.

In a sentence. But Timothy has just now come to us from you and has brought good news about your faith and love. He has told us that you always have pleasant memories of us and that you long to see us, just as we also long to see you. Therefore, brothers and sisters, in all our distress and persecution we were encouraged about you because of your faith.

On a Tuesday. Your faithfulness might be someone else’s comfort. Think of a pastor, parent or mentor who has worried about you. Send them a word this week: tell them how you are doing, and thank them. And when you hear good news of someone’s faith, pass it on; it may be the best thing a weary servant hears all month.

For worship. Thank God for good news of others’ faith, for it is good news of him. Every report of a believer still standing is a report that the gospel is true and the Spirit is at work. The God of all comfort sends his comfort through his people, and he sent it to a frightened apostle in Corinth by the feet of a young man coming down the road. Blessed be the God who comforts the downcast.

verseByVerse.quote: For now we live, if you are standing fast in the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For now we live, if you are standing fast in the Lord.

For now we live, if you are standing fast in the Lord. Twelve words in English, and they are among the most exposed Paul ever wrote. He does not say he is relieved, or encouraged, or grateful, though he is all three. He says he is alive. The months of not knowing had been a kind of death, and Timothy’s news brought him back. A man’s vitality is bound up with whether a church far away is holding.

Love makes you a hostage. Guard it from one misreading. This is not the unhealthy dependence of a leader whose identity rests on how his people are performing. Paul has just spent a chapter insisting he sought no glory from them and would take nothing from them. What he describes is not need but love, and love always makes your wellbeing hostage to someone else’s. That is not a defect in love; it is what love is.

Standing fast. The word is stēkō, the word for a soldier holding his position in the line. Paul uses it repeatedly of churches under pressure (Philippians 1:27; 4:1). It is not a word for advancing or achieving. It means you were still there when the pushing stopped.

In the Lord. And the qualification matters: standing fast in the Lord. Not standing by willpower, or by stubbornness, or by loyalty to Paul. The place they were holding was a person, and their strength was his. The if is also a gentle encouragement: keep standing.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul’s spiritual life depended on them. It expresses how deeply his joy was bound up with them.

What does standing firm look like when I feel weak? It looks like still being there. Standing fast is not feeling strong; it is not leaving your post. It means you keep praying when prayer is dry, keep gathering with God’s people when you would rather stay home, keep refusing the sin that keeps coming back, and keep trusting Christ when you do not understand what he is doing. Because you stand in the Lord, your weakness does not decide the outcome. He holds the line with you.

In a sentence. For now we really live, since you are standing firm in the Lord.

On a Tuesday. There is a plain word here for anybody who thinks their ordinary perseverance is invisible. These were new converts in a provincial city who had, as far as they knew, simply not given up. They had no idea that their not giving up was, at that moment, what an apostle in Corinth was living on. Stand firm in the Lord today. Someone you do not know about is encouraged by it.

For worship. The Lord Jesus is the one in whom his people stand. He stood firm when every disciple fled, and he set his face to Jerusalem and did not turn back. Now he holds his church, and no power can push his people out of the line. The life Paul felt at Timothy’s news is a small echo of the joy of the Good Shepherd, who rejoices over every sheep he keeps.

verseByVerse.quote: For what thanksgiving can we return to God for you, for all the joy that we feel for your sake before our God, as we pray most earnestly night and day that we may see you face to face and supply what is lacking in your faith?
verseByVerse.commentary:
For what thanksgiving can we return to God for you, for all the joy that we feel for your sake before our God, as we pray most earnestly night and day that we may see you face to face and supply what is lacking in your faith?

For what thanksgiving can we return to God for you? It is a real question, not a rhetorical flourish, and Paul does not answer it. He has run out of ways to say thank you. The joy is larger than the vocabulary available for it. And notice to whom the thanks goes: to God, because their faith is God’s work.

For all the joy that we feel for your sake before our God. Note where the joy is felt: before our God. Not merely a private gladness he happens to have, but something he brings into God’s presence and holds up there. Christian joy over other people is a thing you do in front of God, because he is the one who did it.

As we pray most earnestly night and day. The detail is exhausting. The word behind most earnestly (hyperekperissou) is a double superlative: beyond, beyond measure. Paul has stacked the intensifiers because the ordinary ones will not carry it. And night and day is the same phrase he used in 2:9 of working at his trade. Whatever else this man was doing at night, he was not sleeping much.

That we may see you face to face. He prays for two things. First, to see them face to face: the longing of 2:17 has not cooled. Letters are not enough.

And supply what is lacking in your faith? This phrase needs care, because it can sound like a rebuke, and it is not one. Paul has just spent eight verses celebrating their faith. The word is katartizō, and its ordinary uses are physical: to set a broken bone, to mend a torn net (it is the word used of the disciples mending their nets, Matthew 4:21), to put a thing into working order. What is lacking is not sincerity but completeness: the teaching he never got to give because a mob ran him out of town after a month. Chapters 4 and 5 begin to supply it, on holiness, love, and the return of Christ.

What it does not mean. It does not mean their faith was defective. It means it was growing and needed more instruction.

How do I know what is lacking in my faith? There is a deficiency that is a fault, and there is a deficiency that is simply an unfinished education: gaps where nobody ever taught you. Paul’s response to the second is not reproach. It is to want to come and fill them in. So ask honestly: where do I not know what the Bible teaches? Where do I believe but not obey? Where does fear still rule? Then seek the remedy God provides: sit under faithful preaching, read whole books of Scripture, ask a mature believer to help you, and pray for growth. Gaps are expected; staying content with them is not.

Is my faith real if it has gaps? Yes. Every believer’s faith is incomplete in this life. The Thessalonians had a famous faith (1:8) that still lacked things. Real faith is not perfect faith; it is faith that rests on Christ and wants to grow. The fact that you notice gaps and want them filled is itself a sign of life.

In a sentence. How can we thank God enough for you in return for all the joy we have in the presence of our God because of you? Night and day we pray most earnestly that we may see you again and supply what is lacking in your faith.

On a Tuesday. Think of the believers who bring you joy, and bring that joy to God: thank him for them by name, specifically. Then pray for one thing each of them still needs, and if you can supply some of it, a book, a conversation, a Bible study, do.

For worship. The God who began a good work in Thessalonica did not leave it half done; he sent letters, teachers and his own Spirit to complete it. He mends what is torn and sets what is broken, and he will not stop until his people are made whole in the image of his Son. No thanksgiving we can offer is equal to the joy he gives. Glory to the God who finishes what he starts.

verseByVerse.quote: Now may our God and Father himself, and our Lord Jesus, direct our way to you,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now may our God and Father himself, and our Lord Jesus, direct our way to you,

Now may our God and Father himself, and our Lord Jesus. The chapter turns into prayer, and the grammar of this first petition repays a moment. Two subjects, the Father and the Lord Jesus, and in the Greek the verb is singular. Paul names two persons and then speaks of their acting as one. He does not explain it or apologise for it; it is simply how he prays. Alongside the joint preposition of 1:1, it shows how early and how instinctively the highest view of Christ was in place: not as a doctrine being argued, but as the shape of a man’s prayer life. A prayer addressed to the Father and the Son together is a prayer that assumes the Son is God.

Direct our way to you. The verb (kateuthynō) means to make straight, to clear a road. Set it against 2:18, where Satan cut into the road. Paul has named an enemy who blocks the way and now asks the Lord to open it. Both are real in his thinking: the enemy genuinely obstructs, and the Sovereign genuinely governs, and only one of them is being prayed to.

What Paul does with frustration. There is something worth learning in what Paul does with a frustration he has already attributed to Satan. He does not rebuke the devil, and he does not strategise. He asks God to clear the road, and then, as chapter 2 showed, gets on with the work he can do from where he is.

A prayer delayed. The prayer was, in the form he asked it, refused for a long time. So far as we know Paul did not get back to Thessalonica for several years (Acts 20:1–2). What he got instead was Timothy’s report and the opportunity to write this letter, which has done rather more for the church than the visit would have.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the Father and the Son are one person. They are distinct persons who act as one God.

Is it right to pray to Jesus, or only to the Father? Both are right. The usual pattern of Christian prayer is to the Father, through the Son, by the Spirit (Ephesians 2:18). But Scripture also shows believers praying to Jesus directly: Stephen called on him as he died (Acts 7:59), Paul pleaded with the Lord about his thorn (2 Corinthians 12:8), and here he prays to the Father and the Son together. Because the Son is God, he may be addressed in prayer and worshipped. You will not offend the Father by speaking to his Son.

What should I make of it when God does not answer my prayer the way I asked? Keep praying, and keep watching for what he does instead. Paul did not get his visit for years, but God answered the deeper request: the church was strengthened and Paul’s love reached them, through a letter. God always hears his children, and he gives what we would ask for if we knew what he knows. A no or a not yet from a wise Father is still an answer, and often a better one.

In a sentence. Now may our God and Father himself and our Lord Jesus clear the way for us to come to you.

On a Tuesday. Bring the blocked road in your life to God today: the plan that cannot get started, the reunion that keeps failing, the door that will not open. Ask him to direct your way. Then do the work you can do from where you are, and leave the road to him.

For worship. The Father and the Son act as one, and they rule every road on earth. No enemy can close what they open, and no door they shut is shut by accident. The same Lord Jesus who is addressed in this prayer is the way to the Father, and he has made the road to God straight for us by his blood. Blessed be the Father and the Son, one God, who direct our steps.

verseByVerse.quote: and may the Lord make you increase and abound in love for one another and for all, as we do for you, so that he may establish your hearts blameless in holiness before our God and Father, at the coming of our Lord Jesus with all his saints.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and may the Lord make you increase and abound in love for one another and for all, as we do for you, so that he may establish your hearts blameless in holiness before our God and Father, at the coming of our Lord Jesus with all his saints.

And may the Lord make you increase and abound in love. The second petition asks for love, and the verbs are extravagant. The first (pleonazō) means to multiply, to grow more; the second (perisseuō) to overflow the banks. Paul is not asking that they manage to be reasonably loving. He is asking for a flood.

For one another and for all. The direction is deliberate. That second phrase is the sharp one. A community under sustained hostility naturally turns inward: it closes ranks, and its warmth becomes a warmth reserved for insiders. It is entirely understandable, and it is the beginning of a sect. Paul prays that a persecuted church would overflow with love toward the very population making its life difficult, including its persecutors (Matthew 5:44).

As we do for you. Paul offers his own affection as the measure, having spent two chapters demonstrating what it looked like in practice. He can point to it because they watched it.

Who produces it. Notice who is asked to produce this. May the Lord make you increase. Paul does not tell them to try harder at loving people; he asks God to do it in them. He will get to the commands soon enough in chapter 4, but the order here is the order everywhere in his letters: ask God for what you then go and work at.

So that he may establish your hearts blameless in holiness. The whole prayer has an aim. Establish is the buttressing word from verse 2 (stērizō): what Timothy was sent to do, Paul now asks God to do, which is a fair account of how ministry actually works. Love leads to holiness, and blameless means without just accusation. And holiness will be the subject of the very next paragraph (4:3), so the prayer is also the hinge into the letter’s second half.

Before our God and Father. In his presence, at the judgement. The goal of the Christian life is to stand before the Father with nothing that can be justly charged against us.

At the coming of our Lord Jesus with all his saints. Christ’s return, the parousia again. His saints, his holy ones, may be the angels who accompany him (Matthew 25:31), on the pattern of Zechariah 14:5, where the LORD comes and all the holy ones with him; or believers who have died, whom God will bring with him (4:14); or both. Notice what Paul has done: he has borrowed a prophet’s picture of the LORD arriving in judgement and applied it, without comment, to Jesus.

Where Christians differ: coming for his saints, or with them? Some dispensationalists distinguish Christ coming for his saints (a secret rapture) from coming with his saints (seven years later). Verdict: Paul describes one coming, at which Christ brings the souls of departed believers with him, raises their bodies, gathers the living, and judges the world (4:14–17; 2 Thessalonians 1:7–10). He comes both for and with his saints in a single, visible, glorious return. There is no secret rapture.

What it does not mean. It does not mean blamelessness is achieved by us alone. The Lord establishes it.

How can anyone be blameless before God? In two ways, both by grace. First, believers are already counted righteous in Christ: his perfect obedience and his death are credited to them, so that no charge can stand (Romans 8:33–34). Second, God is making them holy in fact, a work he begins at conversion and completes at Christ’s coming, when we shall be like him (1 John 3:2). Paul prays for the second on the basis of the first. You will stand blameless on that day not because you finally got it right, but because Christ did, and because the God who began the work will finish it (5:23–24).

How do I love people who make my life difficult? Start by asking God for it, as Paul does; it is his gift before it is your effort. Then do concrete good: pray for them by name, speak well of them where you honestly can, refuse revenge, and look for a practical kindness. Love is not pretending the harm did not happen, and it does not require you to stay in danger or to trust someone who has not changed. But it does wish them good, and it leaves judgement to God.

In a sentence. May the Lord make your love increase and overflow for each other and for everyone else, just as ours does for you. May he strengthen your hearts so that you will be blameless and holy in the presence of our God and Father when our Lord Jesus comes with all his holy ones.

On a Tuesday. Pray this prayer for your church this week, by name: overflowing love for one another and for all, and hearts established in holiness for Christ’s coming. Then pick one person inside the church and one outside it, and do one loving thing for each. Love now is how a congregation gets ready for then.

For worship. The Lord Jesus is coming with all his holy ones, and the sky will be full of his glory. On that day his people will stand before the Father blameless, not by their own merit but by his blood and his Spirit. Until then he pours his love into hearts that had none, and makes it overflow. Glory to the coming Lord, who will present his church to himself without spot or wrinkle.
